filters.name: Sample Point Cloud by Voxel Grid (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Reduce a point cloud to one averaged point per occupied voxel, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Overlays a regular voxel grid on the cloud and replaces the points in each occupied voxel with their average, producing a new layer. Unlike random or Poisson-disk subsampling this is deterministic and gives a uniform spatial density rather than a uniform count.

Normals and colors are averaged along with the positions when the input carries them; no other per-vertex attribute survives, because the output points are new. Distances are in the layer's own units, not a fraction of its size: a value that suits a scan in millimetres will not suit the same scan in metres.

parameters.label: Voxel Size
parameters.help: Edge length of the cubic grid cells, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. The layer is divided into cells of this size and each occupied cell becomes one point, at the average of the points inside it; their normals and colors are averaged too, and the normals renormalized. Larger cells keep fewer points.

filters.name: Select Point Cloud Outliers by Radius (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Select points with too few neighbours inside a given radius, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Selects every point that has fewer than the required number of neighbours within the search radius. It is a blunt, predictable criterion: it removes isolated specks and sparse haze, and it will also remove genuine geometry wherever the cloud is legitimately sparse.

The points are **selected, not deleted** — inspect the selection and remove it with a Remove filter if it is right. Distances are in the layer's own units, not a fraction of its size: a value that suits a scan in millimetres will not suit the same scan in metres.

parameters.label: Minimum Neighbours
parameters.help: A point with fewer neighbours than this inside the search radius is selected.

parameters.label: Search Radius
parameters.help: Radius of the sphere searched around each point, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal.

filters.name: Select Point Cloud Outliers Statistically (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Select points whose mean neighbour distance is an outlier, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Computes the mean distance from each point to its *k* nearest neighbours, then selects every point whose mean lies further than the given number of standard deviations above the global average. Unlike the radius criterion this adapts to the cloud's own density, so it suits a scan whose sampling varies across the surface.

The points are **selected, not deleted**.

parameters.label: Neighbour Count
parameters.help: How many nearest neighbours the mean distance is computed over.

parameters.label: Standard Deviations
parameters.help: How far above the global average a point's mean neighbour distance must lie before it is selected. Lower values select more points.

filters.name: Compute Point Cloud Normals (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Estimate per-vertex normals from a point cloud's local neighbourhoods, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Fits a plane to the neighbourhood of each point and takes its normal, through the covariance of the neighbours. Three neighbourhood definitions are offered: a fixed count, a fixed radius, or a hybrid that takes the nearer of the two.

**The result is unoriented.** Plane fitting determines a normal's line, not its sign, so adjacent normals may point to opposite sides of the surface — which is fatal for Ball Pivoting and for any lighting. Enable consistent orientation to resolve this with a minimum spanning tree over the tangent planes, or use one of the Orient filters afterwards. Distances are in the layer's own units, not a fraction of its size: a value that suits a scan in millimetres will not suit the same scan in metres.

parameters.label: Neighbourhood
parameters.help: How the neighbourhood of each point is chosen.

enumOptions.label: Nearest Neighbours
enumOptions.help: A fixed number of nearest neighbours. Adapts to density; the only mode that needs no radius.

enumOptions.label: Radius
enumOptions.help: Every neighbour within the search radius. Fails where the cloud is sparser than the radius.

enumOptions.label: Hybrid
enumOptions.help: Nearest neighbours, but no further than the search radius. Open3D's own default for scan data.

parameters.label: Neighbour Count
parameters.help: How many nearest neighbours to fit the plane over. Ignored in Radius mode.

parameters.label: Search Radius
parameters.help: Neighbourhood radius for the Radius and Hybrid modes, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal.

parameters.label: Orient consistently
parameters.help: Propagate a consistent sign across the cloud with a minimum spanning tree over the tangent planes. Costs more time, and is what Ball Pivoting needs.

parameters.label: Fast normal computation
parameters.help: Use Open3D's faster eigenvector approximation rather than a full eigen decomposition. Turn it off if the normals look unstable in near-planar regions.

filters.name: Reconstruct Surface by Ball Pivoting (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Reconstruct a surface by rolling balls of several radii over an oriented point cloud, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
Rolls a ball across the oriented points; wherever it rests on three without containing any other, those three become a triangle. The result interpolates the input points rather than approximating them, so it keeps the original samples exactly — the opposite trade from Poisson reconstruction, which smooths and is watertight.

**Several radii, applied in increasing order.** Each pass bridges what the previous ball was too large to enter, so a list covers a cloud of uneven density where one radius cannot. Leaving the list empty derives four radii from the layer's bounding box diagonal, which is a starting point rather than a good answer for any particular scan.

The input must carry **oriented** normals; the filter refuses without them. Expect holes where the cloud is sparser than the largest ball: this method does not close them, and does not claim to be watertight.

parameters.label: Ball Radii
parameters.help: Ball radii, in increasing order, separated by spaces or commas — for example "0.5 1 2". Leave empty to derive four radii from the bounding box diagonal. Distances are in the layer's own units, not a fraction of its size: a value that suits a scan in millimetres will not suit the same scan in metres.

filters.name: Align Layer to Reference by Point-to-Point ICP (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Register two layers by minimizing distances between corresponding points, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
**Starting alignment:** the layers must already be roughly aligned. ICP refines a pose; it cannot find one. Each source point is paired with its nearest reference point within the maximum correspondence distance, so the overlap has to start within that distance of where it belongs. If the layers start far apart or turned, run *Align Layer to Reference by RANSAC Feature Matching* first.

Iteratively pairs each source point with the nearest reference point and minimizes the sum of squared distances between the pairs. The classic Besl-McKay objective: it needs no normals and makes no assumption about the surface, which also makes it the slowest to converge on smooth geometry, where sliding along the surface costs it nothing.

The **current layer** is the one that moves, and the reference layer stays put. The result is written to the current layer's **matrix**, composed onto whatever it already carried; the vertex coordinates are not touched. Fitness (the fraction of source points that found a correspondence) and inlier RMSE are reported so the result can be judged rather than assumed.

parameters.label: Reference Mesh
parameters.help: The layer the current layer is moved onto. It stays put.

parameters.label: Maximum Correspondence Distance
parameters.help: Points further apart than this are never paired, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. Larger values tolerate a rougher starting alignment; too large lets distant surfaces pair with each other.

parameters.label: Maximum Iterations
parameters.help: Upper bound on ICP iterations; it stops earlier once fitness and RMSE settle.

parameters.label: Estimate scale
parameters.help: Also solve for a uniform scale factor. Leave off unless the two layers genuinely differ in scale: a free scale can absorb a bad alignment and report a good fitness.

filters.name: Align Layer to Reference by Point-to-Plane ICP (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Register two layers by minimizing point-to-tangent-plane distances, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
**Starting alignment:** the layers must already be roughly aligned. ICP refines a pose; it cannot find one. Each source point is paired with its nearest reference point within the maximum correspondence distance, so the overlap has to start within that distance of where it belongs. If the layers start far apart or turned, run *Align Layer to Reference by RANSAC Feature Matching* first.

Minimizes the distance from each source point to the *tangent plane* at its corresponding reference point, rather than to the point itself. Sliding along a smooth surface is then free of penalty only in the directions the surface actually permits, so it converges in far fewer iterations than point-to-point on scan data.

The reference layer must carry normals; the filter refuses without them.

The **current layer** is the one that moves, and the reference layer stays put. The result is written to the current layer's **matrix**, composed onto whatever it already carried; the vertex coordinates are not touched. Fitness (the fraction of source points that found a correspondence) and inlier RMSE are reported so the result can be judged rather than assumed.

parameters.label: Reference Mesh
parameters.help: The layer the current layer is moved onto. It stays put.

parameters.label: Maximum Correspondence Distance
parameters.help: Points further apart than this are never paired, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. Larger values tolerate a rougher starting alignment; too large lets distant surfaces pair with each other.

parameters.label: Maximum Iterations
parameters.help: Upper bound on ICP iterations; it stops earlier once fitness and RMSE settle.

filters.name: Align Layer to Reference by Colored ICP (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Register two colored layers using both geometry and color, with Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
**Starting alignment:** the layers must already be roughly aligned. ICP refines a pose; it cannot find one. Each source point is paired with its nearest reference point within the maximum correspondence distance, so the overlap has to start within that distance of where it belongs. If the layers start far apart or turned, run *Align Layer to Reference by RANSAC Feature Matching* first.

Adds a photometric term to the point-to-plane objective, so color gradients constrain the motion that geometry alone leaves ambiguous. This is the case it exists for: a flat painted wall, or a cylinder free to slide and spin, where a purely geometric ICP has nothing to hold on to.

Both layers need per-vertex color, and both need normals.

The **current layer** is the one that moves, and the reference layer stays put. The result is written to the current layer's **matrix**, composed onto whatever it already carried; the vertex coordinates are not touched. Fitness (the fraction of source points that found a correspondence) and inlier RMSE are reported so the result can be judged rather than assumed.

parameters.label: Reference Mesh
parameters.help: The layer the current layer is moved onto. It stays put.

parameters.label: Maximum Correspondence Distance
parameters.help: Points further apart than this are never paired, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. Larger values tolerate a rougher starting alignment; too large lets distant surfaces pair with each other.

parameters.label: Maximum Iterations
parameters.help: Upper bound on ICP iterations; it stops earlier once fitness and RMSE settle.

filters.name: Align Layer to Reference by RANSAC Feature Matching (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Find a coarse pose between two layers from FPFH descriptors and RANSAC, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
**Starting alignment:** none. The layers may start in any position and orientation, because the pose is found from surface shape alone and not from where the layers currently are. What it does need is real surface overlap, and normals on both layers. The result is a coarse pose (on one pair of range maps it landed within about 2% of the bounding-box diagonal); refine it with ICP.

Describes every point by a Fast Point Feature Histogram of its neighbours' relative orientations, matches those descriptors between the two layers, and fits a pose to the matches with RANSAC.

**This is an initializer, not a final alignment** — the name follows the verb lexicon, where *Align* means deriving a registration transform, but the result is coarse. It needs no starting pose at all, which is exactly what ICP cannot do — but it returns a coarse result. Run one of the ICP filters afterwards to refine it.

Both layers need normals, since the descriptor is built from them.

**Both layers are downsampled before matching**, controlled by the matching voxel size. Global registration is defined on a sparse cloud: every RANSAC iteration transforms the whole source cloud and searches the target for each point, so a raw scan costs minutes where a few thousand points cost seconds — for the same pose, since a rigid transform does not depend on sampling density. Refine with an ICP filter afterwards, which does run at full resolution.

**A set of layers can be the reference.** With *Use All Visible Layers as Reference* the target is every other visible layer combined, in world space, so the current layer can be placed against whichever of them it overlaps. This is what a scan sequence needs when a new scan overlaps the surface already built up but not the scan just before it -- for instance the first scan of a second loop around the object. The combined points go through the same downsampling as a single layer, so surface covered by several scans is not counted several times. Every layer in the set needs normals. Hide the layers that should not take part.

The **current layer** is the one that moves, and the reference layer stays put. The result is written to the current layer's **matrix**, composed onto whatever it already carried; the vertex coordinates are not touched. Fitness (the fraction of source points that found a correspondence) and inlier RMSE are reported so the result can be judged rather than assumed.

**How good is the guess?** RANSAC scores its own pose on the downsampled clouds, which flatters it. Turn on *Estimate Quality with ICP* to also score the pose on the full layers and to run ICP from it, at full resolution, for an estimate that is not limited by the downsampling: the log reports the fitness and inlier RMSE before and after ICP, and how far ICP moved the pose in degrees and as a share of the diagonal. A pose that ICP leaves almost where it was is a good one; a large move, or a large gain in fitness, says the guess was rough and an ICP filter should follow. The ICP result itself is not applied. The same figures are returned as output values to a script (`fitness`, `inlier_rmse`, `inlier_correspondences`, and with the option `full_fitness`, `full_inlier_rmse`, `icp_fitness`, `icp_inlier_rmse`, `icp_rotation_degrees`, `icp_translation` and `icp_translation_percent_of_diagonal`).

parameters.label: Reference Mesh
parameters.help: The layer the current layer is moved onto. It stays put.

parameters.label: Use All Visible Layers as Reference
parameters.help: Take every other visible layer together as the reference instead of the one named above, which is then ignored. Their points are combined and downsampled internally. Use it when the current layer overlaps the scans already placed but not the one before it in the sequence.

parameters.label: Maximum Correspondence Distance
parameters.help: A point within this distance of its match counts as matched: it decides which candidate poses are accepted and the fitness reported. In the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal.

parameters.label: Downsampling Cell Size
parameters.help: Edge length of the cubic grid cells, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. Both layers are reduced to one point per occupied cell, at the average of its points, before descriptors are computed and matched; the pose found is applied to the full layers. Fine cells are slow and coarse ones lose the pose: on one pair of range maps 0.25% of the diagonal took 76 s, 1% took 0.15 s and 8% failed. The default keeps about 4,500 points of 80,000.

parameters.label: Feature Radius
parameters.help: Radius of the neighbourhood each descriptor is computed over, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. Larger values describe more context and match more robustly, at more cost. It is not tied to the matching voxel size: the defaults (5% and 1% of the diagonal) are the ones tested together, and scaling both with a larger voxel made matching worse at 2% and 4%.

parameters.label: Feature Neighbours
parameters.help: Upper bound on neighbours per descriptor, within the feature radius.

parameters.label: Mutual filter
parameters.help: Keep only correspondences that are each other's best match in both directions. Fewer and better matches, which usually helps RANSAC rather than hindering it.

parameters.label: Estimate Quality with ICP
parameters.help: After the coarse pose is found, measure it again on the full-resolution layers and run point-to-plane ICP from it, and report both scores and how far ICP had to move the pose. A pose that ICP barely moves, and that scores about the same afterwards, was a good guess; one it moves a lot, or that scores much better, was a rough one. The ICP result is only measured, not applied: the layers carry the coarse pose, and refining it is the job of the ICP filters. Costs one ICP run at full resolution. The numbers are also in the result's output values, for a script.

parameters.label: RANSAC Iterations
parameters.help: Upper bound on RANSAC samples; it stops earlier once the confidence is reached.

parameters.label: RANSAC Confidence
parameters.help: Probability of having found the best model, at which sampling stops.

parameters.label: Random Seed
parameters.help: Seed for the random sampling this method does. Zero draws a fresh seed each run and reports it, so a result can be reproduced afterwards by pinning that value. Two runs with the same seed give the same pose; two runs with different seeds may not.

filters.name: Align Sets by RANSAC Feature Matching (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Find a coarse pose between two visibility sets of layers from FPFH descriptors and RANSAC, and move the whole moving set by it, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
**Starting alignment:** none. The two sets may start in any position and orientation, because the pose is found from surface shape alone and not from where the layers currently are. What it needs is real surface overlap between the two sets, and normals on every layer. The result is a coarse pose; refine it with ICP.

This is *Align Layer to Reference by RANSAC Feature Matching* with a **visibility set** on each side instead of a layer. Each set is taken as one rigid group: the points of its layers are put together in world space, each through its own matrix, and downsampled by the matching voxel size (so surface covered by several layers is not counted several times). FPFH descriptors are computed on the two groups, matched, and a pose is fitted with RANSAC.

**Every layer of the moving set gets the same correction**, composed onto the matrix it already has, so the set keeps its internal alignment and moves as a whole; the reference set stays put and no vertex coordinates are touched. This is what two groups of scans, each already aligned within itself, need to be joined, when no single scan of one group overlaps enough of the other to be registered on its own.

Make the sets in the layer panel: show the layers that belong together and press **+** under the list. A layer cannot be in both sets, and a layer with no vertices is left out. Fitness (the fraction of source points that found a correspondence) and inlier RMSE are reported so the result can be judged rather than assumed.

On success the two sets together are left as a new visibility set called *aligned* (*aligned 2* and so on if that name is taken), so the joined group is one click away.

**How good is the guess?** RANSAC scores its own pose on the downsampled clouds, which flatters it. Turn on *Estimate Quality with ICP* to also score the pose on the full layers and to run ICP from it, at full resolution, for an estimate that is not limited by the downsampling: the log reports the fitness and inlier RMSE before and after ICP, and how far ICP moved the pose in degrees and as a share of the diagonal. A pose that ICP leaves almost where it was is a good one; a large move, or a large gain in fitness, says the guess was rough and an ICP filter should follow. The ICP result itself is not applied. The same figures are returned as output values to a script (`fitness`, `inlier_rmse`, `inlier_correspondences`, and with the option `full_fitness`, `full_inlier_rmse`, `icp_fitness`, `icp_inlier_rmse`, `icp_rotation_degrees`, `icp_translation` and `icp_translation_percent_of_diagonal`).

parameters.label: Moving Set
parameters.help: The visibility set that is moved. Its layers move together, all by the same correction, so they stay as they are relative to each other. Make the set with the + under the layer list, or let a filter leave one (Align Meshes Sequentially leaves *aligned*).

parameters.label: Reference Set
parameters.help: The visibility set the moving set is placed against. It stays put. A layer cannot be in both sets.

parameters.label: Maximum Correspondence Distance
parameters.help: A point within this distance of its match counts as matched: it decides which candidate poses are accepted and the fitness reported. In the layers' units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal.

parameters.label: Downsampling Cell Size
parameters.help: Edge length of the cubic grid cells, in the layers' units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. The points of each set are reduced to one point per occupied cell, at the average of its points, before descriptors are computed and matched; the pose found is applied to the full layers of the moving set. Fine cells are slow and coarse ones lose the pose: on one pair of range maps 0.25% of the diagonal took 76 s, 1% took 0.15 s and 8% failed. The default keeps about 4,500 points of 80,000.

parameters.label: Feature Radius
parameters.help: Radius of the neighbourhood each descriptor is computed over, in the layers' units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. Larger values describe more context and match more robustly, at more cost. It is not tied to the matching voxel size: the defaults (5% and 1% of the diagonal) are the ones tested together, and scaling both with a larger voxel made matching worse at 2% and 4%.

parameters.label: Feature Neighbours
parameters.help: Upper bound on neighbours per descriptor, within the feature radius.

parameters.label: Mutual filter
parameters.help: Keep only correspondences that are each other's best match in both directions. Fewer and better matches, which usually helps RANSAC rather than hindering it.

parameters.label: Estimate Quality with ICP
parameters.help: After the coarse pose is found, measure it again on the full-resolution layers and run point-to-plane ICP from it, and report both scores and how far ICP had to move the pose. A pose that ICP barely moves, and that scores about the same afterwards, was a good guess; one it moves a lot, or that scores much better, was a rough one. The ICP result is only measured, not applied: the layers carry the coarse pose, and refining it is the job of the ICP filters. Costs one ICP run at full resolution. The numbers are also in the result's output values, for a script.

parameters.label: RANSAC Iterations
parameters.help: Upper bound on RANSAC samples; it stops earlier once the confidence is reached.

parameters.label: RANSAC Confidence
parameters.help: Probability of having found the best model, at which sampling stops.

parameters.label: Random Seed
parameters.help: Seed for the random sampling this method does. Zero draws a fresh seed each run and reports it, so a result can be reproduced afterwards by pinning that value. Two runs with the same seed give the same pose; two runs with different seeds may not.

filters.name: Align Layer to Reference by Fast Global Registration (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Find a coarse pose between two layers (or a layer and all the visible ones) from FPFH descriptors without RANSAC, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
**Starting alignment:** any position, but a limited rotation. The method removes each layer's centre and then refines the rotation starting from the identity, so it does not care where the layers sit but does depend on how they are turned. It registered a turntable pair roughly 45 degrees apart, and failed on a later pair of the same scans once the reference had been moved into place and the next scan had not; the limit between the two is not characterised. For layers in arbitrary orientation use *Align Layer to Reference by RANSAC Feature Matching*.

Matches the same FPFH descriptors as *Align Layer to Reference by RANSAC Feature Matching*, then — instead of sampling candidate poses with RANSAC — optimizes a robust objective over all correspondences at once, annealing the scale parameter downward so that wrong matches lose influence as the solution settles (graduated non-convexity).

The practical difference is cost: there is no iteration budget to guess at, and no sampling to get unlucky with. It is usually the faster of the two for the same pair. RANSAC remains the more conservative choice where overlap is low, which is why both are offered rather than one replacing the other.

**This is an initializer.** Like the RANSAC route it needs no starting pose, and like it the result is coarse — refine with one of the ICP filters, which run at full resolution.

Both layers need normals, since the descriptor is built from them, and both are downsampled before matching for the same reason as the RANSAC route.

**The reference can be every other visible layer**, as with the RANSAC route: with *Use All Visible Layers as Reference* the target is those layers combined in world space, and *Reference Mesh* is ignored. The parameters of the two routes are the same where the methods share a step (the matching distance, the downsampling, the descriptors, the visible-layers reference, the quality estimate) and differ only in what each method needs of its own.

The **current layer** is the one that moves, and the reference layer stays put. The result is written to the current layer's **matrix**, composed onto whatever it already carried; the vertex coordinates are not touched. Fitness and inlier RMSE are reported.

**How good is the pose?** Turn on *Estimate Quality with ICP* to score the pose on the full layers and to run ICP from it, without applying the ICP result: the log reports the fitness and inlier RMSE before and after, and how far ICP moved the pose. A pose ICP barely moves was a good one. Use it when the current layer overlaps the scans already placed but not the one before it in the sequence. Hide the layers that should not take part.

parameters.label: Downsampling Cell Size

parameters.label: Feature Neighbours
parameters.help: Upper bound on neighbours per descriptor, within the feature radius.

parameters.label: Iterations
parameters.help: Annealing rounds. Each one lowers the scale parameter by the division factor.

parameters.label: Estimate Quality with ICP
parameters.help: After the coarse pose is found, measure it again on the full-resolution layers and run point-to-plane ICP from it, and report both scores and how far ICP had to move the pose. A pose that ICP barely moves, and that scores about the same afterwards, was a good guess; one it moves a lot, or that scores much better, was a rough one. parameters.label: Division Factor
parameters.help: How fast the scale parameter anneals. Larger values converge sooner and are less tolerant of wrong correspondences.

parameters.label: Anneal the scale parameter
parameters.help: Lower the scale parameter each round, which is what graduated non-convexity means. Turning it off keeps a fixed robustness scale throughout.

parameters.label: Tuple Scale
parameters.help: Similarity tolerance when testing triples of correspondences for geometric compatibility.

parameters.label: Maximum Tuple Count
parameters.help: Upper bound on the compatible triples kept from the initial correspondences.

parameters.label: Geometric compatibility test
parameters.help: Discard correspondence triples whose relative distances disagree between the two layers. Cheap, and it removes most wrong matches before the optimization starts.

parameters.label: Random Seed
parameters.help: Seed for the random sampling this method does. Zero draws a fresh seed each run and reports it, so a result can be reproduced afterwards by pinning that value. Two runs with the same seed give the same pose; two runs with different seeds may not.

filters.shortDescription: Find a coarse pose between two visibility sets of layers from FPFH descriptors without RANSAC, and move the whole moving set by it, using Open3D.

A layer cannot be in both sets, and a layer with no vertices is left out. Make the sets in the layer panel: show the layers that belong together and press **+** under the list.

On success the two sets together are left as a new visibility set called *aligned* (*aligned 2* and so on if that name is taken). Fitness and inlier RMSE are reported; *Estimate Quality with ICP* adds the full-layer scores and how far ICP would move the pose, as for the other aligners, with the same output values.

parameters.label: Moving Set
parameters.help: The visibility set that is moved. Its layers move together, all by the same correction, so they stay as they are relative to each other. Make the set with the + under the layer list, or let a filter leave one (Align Meshes Sequentially leaves *aligned*).

parameters.label: Reference Set
parameters.help: The visibility set the moving set is placed against. It stays put. A layer cannot be in both sets.

parameters.label: Maximum Correspondence Distance
parameters.help: A point within this distance of its match counts as matched: it decides which candidate poses are accepted and the fitness reported. In the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal.

parameters.label: Downsampling Cell Size
parameters.help: Edge length of the cubic grid cells, in the layers' units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. The points of each set are reduced to one point per occupied cell, at the average of its points, before descriptors are computed and matched; the pose found is applied to the full layers of the moving set. Fine cells are slow and coarse ones lose the pose: on one pair of range maps 0.25% of the diagonal took 76 s, 1% took 0.15 s and 8% failed. The default keeps about 4,500 points of 80,000.

parameters.label: Feature Radius
parameters.help: Radius of the neighbourhood each descriptor is computed over, in the layers' units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. Larger values describe more context and match more robustly, at more cost. It is not tied to the matching voxel size: the defaults (5% and 1% of the diagonal) are the ones tested together, and scaling both with a larger voxel made matching worse at 2% and 4%.

parameters.label: Feature Neighbours
parameters.help: Upper bound on neighbours per descriptor, within the feature radius.

parameters.label: Iterations
parameters.help: Annealing rounds. Each one lowers the scale parameter by the division factor.

parameters.label: Estimate Quality with ICP
parameters.help: After the coarse pose is found, measure it again on the full-resolution layers and run point-to-plane ICP from it, and report both scores and how far ICP had to move the pose. A pose that ICP barely moves, and that scores about the same afterwards, was a good guess; one it moves a lot, or that scores much better, was a rough one. The ICP result is only measured, not applied: the layers carry the coarse pose, and refining it is the job of the ICP filters. Costs one ICP run at full resolution. The numbers are also in the result's output values, for a script.

parameters.label: Division Factor
parameters.help: How fast the scale parameter anneals. Larger values converge sooner and are less tolerant of wrong correspondences.

parameters.label: Anneal the scale parameter
parameters.help: Lower the scale parameter each round, which is what graduated non-convexity means. Turning it off keeps a fixed robustness scale throughout.

parameters.label: Tuple Scale
parameters.help: Similarity tolerance when testing triples of correspondences for geometric compatibility.

parameters.label: Maximum Tuple Count
parameters.help: Upper bound on the compatible triples kept from the initial correspondences.

parameters.label: Geometric compatibility test
parameters.help: Discard correspondence triples whose relative distances disagree between the two layers. Cheap, and it removes most wrong matches before the optimization starts.

parameters.label: Random Seed
parameters.help: Seed for the random sampling this method does. Zero draws a fresh seed each run and reports it, so a result can be reproduced afterwards by pinning that value. Two runs with the same seed give the same pose; two runs with different seeds may not.

filters.name: Align Meshes Globally (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Align many overlapping layers at once by optimizing a pose graph, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
**Starting alignment:** depends on *Pair Initialization*. With *Current Pose* (the default) the layers must already be roughly placed, close enough that ICP converges on each overlapping pair; *Align Meshes Sequentially* is the way to get them there. With *RANSAC Feature Matching* none is needed, at a higher cost; with *Fast Global Registration* none is needed either, at a lower one, but the layers must be roughly oriented alike. Layer order does not matter.

Registers every overlapping pair of layers, assembles the results into a **pose graph** — one node per layer, one edge per accepted pair — and optimizes all the poses together with Levenberg-Marquardt.

This is what a chain of pairwise ICP cannot do. Aligning A to B, then B to C, then C to D accumulates drift and has nowhere to put the disagreement when D also overlaps A. The global optimization distributes that error across the whole graph instead.

Every edge is treated as a **loop closure** rather than trusted odometry, because layers in a document carry no scan order. Open3D's line process then down-weights and prunes edges that disagree with the consensus, so one bad pairwise registration degrades the result rather than wrecking it. Pairs that register below the minimum fitness are rejected before they ever reach the graph.

Only the layer **matrices** change; no coordinates are touched, and the reference layer is held fixed so the whole group does not drift in world space.

**Pair initialization is the choice that matters most.** By default each pairwise registration refines the relative pose the layers already have, which is right once they are roughly placed and useless before that — ICP cannot find a pose it is not already near. Setting it to *RANSAC Feature Matching* or to *Fast Global Registration* computes each pair's pose from FPFH descriptors first, so **no prior placement is needed at all** (with the orientation limit of the second). This mirrors Open3D's own `register_fragments` pipeline, which treats consecutive frames as known odometry and finds every other pair by global registration.

Either descriptor-based choice also forces every pair to be attempted: a bounding-box overlap test asks where the layers are, and that is precisely what is unknown. Descriptors are computed once per layer and reused across pairs.

Cost grows with the number of pairs, which is quadratic in the layer count. With poses already trusted, the default considers only pairs whose bounding boxes overlap, which is usually most of the saving.

parameters.label: Reference Mesh
parameters.help: The layer held fixed. Everything else moves around it, so the group keeps its place in world space.

parameters.label: Only visible layers
parameters.help: Align only the layers currently visible. Turn off to include hidden ones.

parameters.label: Pair Initialization
parameters.help: Where each pairwise registration starts from.

enumOptions.label: Current Layer Poses
enumOptions.help: Refine the relative pose the layers already have. Correct when they are roughly placed already — after a manual or sequential alignment — and useless before that.

enumOptions.label: RANSAC Feature Matching (automatic)
enumOptions.help: Find each pair's pose from FPFH features by RANSAC, ignoring where the layers currently sit, then refine it. No prior placement is needed and the orientation of the layers does not matter, but every pair that does not match spends the whole RANSAC iteration budget, and the pairs are quadratic in the layers: lower *RANSAC Iterations* for many layers. It forces every pair to be attempted, since bounding boxes cannot be trusted to overlap yet.

enumOptions.label: Fast Global Registration (automatic)
enumOptions.help: Find each pair's pose from FPFH features by Fast Global Registration, ignoring where the layers currently sit, then refine it. Much cheaper than RANSAC and with no sampling budget, but it optimizes the rotation from the identity, so the layers must be roughly oriented alike (position does not matter). It forces every pair to be attempted.

parameters.label: Candidate Pairs
parameters.help: Which pairs of layers to attempt a registration between.

enumOptions.label: Overlapping Bounding Boxes
enumOptions.help: Only pairs whose world-space bounding boxes intersect. A cheap test that skips pairs which cannot possibly register.

enumOptions.label: All Pairs
enumOptions.help: Every pair. Thorough, and quadratic in the layer count: use it when layers start far from their true poses, so that bounding boxes do not yet overlap.

parameters.label: Maximum Correspondence Distance
parameters.help: Pairing distance for the pairwise registrations and for the line process, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal.

parameters.label: Downsampling Cell Size
parameters.help: Edge length of the cubic grid cells, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. Each layer is reduced to one point per occupied cell, at the average of its points, before pairing; the pairwise ICP and the pose graph run on those points. Every pair costs time proportional to the point count.

parameters.label: Minimum Pair Fitness
parameters.help: A pairwise registration below this fitness is discarded rather than added as an edge. Raising it admits fewer and better edges; too high and the graph stops being connected.

parameters.label: Pairwise ICP Iterations
parameters.help: Iteration cap for each pairwise registration.

parameters.label: Loop Closure Preference
parameters.help: How strongly the optimizer favours loop-closure edges over leaving poses where they are. Open3D recommends 2.0 for registering fragments and 0.1 for RGB-D odometry.

parameters.label: Edge Prune Threshold
parameters.help: Edges whose line-process weight falls below this are pruned as outliers.

parameters.label: RANSAC Iterations
parameters.help: Upper bound on RANSAC samples for each pair, with *RANSAC Feature Matching* as the pair initialization; ignored otherwise. A pair that matches stops earlier; one that does not spends all of it, so lower it for many layers.

parameters.label: Random Seed
parameters.help: Seed for the random sampling this method does. Zero draws a fresh seed each run and reports it, so a result can be reproduced afterwards by pinning that value. Two runs with the same seed give the same pose; two runs with different seeds may not.

filters.name: Align Meshes Sequentially (Open3D)
filters.shortDescription: Align a sequence of overlapping scans one after another from raw positions, restart the chain after a pair that fails, and optimize each aligned group, using Open3D.
filters.longDescriptionMarkdown:
**Starting alignment:** none with the default method. Only the reference stays where it is; every later layer may start in any position and orientation. (With *Fast Global Registration* as the coarse method, each layer must be roughly oriented like the one before it; position still does not matter.) What the filter does need is that the layers are listed in scanning order, so that **each one overlaps the one before it**, and that every layer has normals. Meshes loaded from a file get smooth normals automatically when the file has none; a point cloud needs *Compute Point Cloud Normals* first.

Starting from the reference layer, it takes each following layer in the layer list and moves it onto the one before it: a coarse pose from *Align Layer to Reference by RANSAC Feature Matching* or, with *Coarse Alignment* set to it, from *Align Layer to Reference by Fast Global Registration*, then *Align Layer to Reference by Point-to-Plane ICP* to refine it. Each pair it attempts is written to the log, with the fitness it reached. This is the sequence Open3D's `register_fragments` tutorial describes, and what registering a set of range maps one by one by hand amounts to.

**What a layer is registered onto** is a choice, *Reference*. By default it is the layer before it, which needs each layer to overlap its predecessor. *All Previously Aligned Layers* uses the whole group placed so far as one reference at every step: a layer can then join through any layer already placed, as the first scan of a second loop around an object overlaps the first loop but not the scan just before it, and each layer is anchored to everything built up instead of to one scan. *Previous Layer, then All Aligned on Failure* keeps the cheap default and falls back to the whole group only for a layer that did not register onto its predecessor, before the chain restarts from it.

**A pair that fails is tried again, then starts a new group.** A pair is judged after ICP has refined it: it fails if the registration finds no correspondences, if its fitness is below the minimum, or if its inlier RMSE is above the maximum pair error. It is then tried again with another seed, up to *Attempts per Pair* times in all, since both coarse methods sample at random. If every attempt fails, the pair ends the group being built. The layer that failed is put back where it was found and becomes the reference of the layers after it, which are aligned onto it in turn: the chain restarts from it rather than giving up. Each group of two or more layers is optimized together with *Align Meshes Globally*, so the drift a chain accumulates is shared across the group instead of being left in its last layer. Turn *Global Refinement* off to keep each chain as it stands.

Groups are not placed relative to one another, because nothing overlapped across the break; each is aligned onto its own first layer. The log and the result name every failure with its reason, and every group. To join two groups, use *Align Sets by RANSAC Feature Matching* on the sets the run leaves, or place one by hand.

The feature matcher samples randomly. Every pair of a run uses the same *Random Seed*, which is reported, so a run can be replayed.

Layers listed *before* the reference are not part of the chain and are not touched. Only layer matrices change; no coordinates are modified.

Each group is left as a **visibility set** under the layer list, the group's first layer among its layers: *aligned* for the first, then *aligned 2*, *aligned 3* and so on (a name already taken gets a number, as a layer's does). One click shows exactly what a group placed and hides the layers left out. A layer that registered with neither neighbour is in no set. The run fails, moving nothing, only if no pair registered at all.

parameters.label: Starting Reference Mesh
parameters.help: The first layer of the chain. It stays where it is, and each later layer in the layer list is aligned onto the one before it. Layers listed before it are not touched.

parameters.label: Only visible layers
parameters.help: Skip hidden layers. Turn off to include them in the chain.

parameters.label: Coarse Alignment
parameters.help: How each pair gets its starting pose, before ICP refines it.

enumOptions.label: RANSAC Feature Matching
enumOptions.help: Samples candidate poses from the matched FPFH descriptors. The conservative choice: it has no limit on how the two layers are turned relative to each other, and copes with low overlap, at the cost of a sampling budget.

enumOptions.label: Fast Global Registration
enumOptions.help: Optimizes a robust objective over all the matched descriptors at once, with no sampling. Usually faster, and deterministic for a given seed, but it optimizes the rotation from the identity, so each layer must be roughly oriented like the one before it (position does not matter). Fine for scans of a turntable or a walk-around, where consecutive views differ by a step; use RANSAC when they may be turned arbitrarily.

parameters.label: Reference
parameters.help: What each layer is registered onto.

enumOptions.label: Previous Layer
enumOptions.help: The layer before it in the list, only. Cheap, and each pair is a clean two-layer registration, but every layer must overlap its predecessor enough to register, and the error accumulates along the chain.

enumOptions.label: All Previously Aligned Layers
enumOptions.help: The whole group placed so far, taken together as one reference, at every step. More surface to overlap, so a layer can join through any of the layers already placed, and each is anchored to everything built up rather than to one scan; the reference grows with the group, so each step costs more. Every layer needs normals.

enumOptions.label: Previous Layer, then All Aligned on Failure
enumOptions.help: The layer before it first; only if that fails (after its attempts), the whole group placed so far, with its own attempts, before the chain restarts from that layer. Costs nothing on pairs that register, and rescues a layer that overlaps the group but not its predecessor.

parameters.label: Minimum Pair Fitness
parameters.help: A pair whose ICP fitness (the fraction of source points with a correspondence) falls below this fails, and the chain restarts from that layer. Registered range maps reached 0.8 or more; a pair that did not register read 0.24. Lower it for scans with little overlap.

parameters.label: Maximum Pair Error
parameters.help: After ICP has refined a pair, its inlier RMSE -- how far, on average, the matched points lie from the reference surface -- must stay under this, as a percentage of the reference layer's bounding-box diagonal; otherwise the pair fails. It catches a pose that covers enough of the surface to pass the fitness test and still sits visibly off it: on range maps that registered the error was 0.35% to 0.56% of the diagonal, and a side scan that only seemed to register read 0.95%. Zero turns the check off. Raise it for noisy scans.

parameters.label: Maximum Correspondence Distance
parameters.help: Pairing distance for every pairwise registration and for the final optimization, in the layer's units, and also as a percentage of the current layer's bounding-box diagonal. The same value is used for every pair.

parameters.label: ICP Iterations
parameters.help: Iteration cap for the ICP refinement of each pair, and for the pairwise registrations of the final optimization.

parameters.label: Attempts per Pair
parameters.help: How many times a pair is tried before the chain gives up on it and restarts from that layer. The coarse methods sample at random, so another seed can succeed where one failed: each attempt uses the seed plus its number, so the run stays reproducible. A pair is accepted at the first attempt that passes both the fitness and the pair-error checks. Each failed attempt costs a full registration. 1 means no retry.

parameters.label: Global Refinement
parameters.help: After each group of the chain is built, optimize all the layers it placed together. Needs at least three layers in the group to have anything to distribute.

parameters.label: Random Seed
parameters.help: Seed for the feature matching of every pair. Zero draws one fresh seed for the whole run and reports it, so the run can be replayed by pinning that value.
